```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

# Anchor here() to this post so paths work no matter where R starts
here::i_am("posts/welcome/index.qmd")

# House colours, ggplot2 theme, and the packages every post uses
source(here::here("R", "theme_cwr.R"))

# Data download bundle helpers; data_bundle_version is the release version linked at the end.
# Bump it when the data changes and /publish rebuilds the bundle.
source(here::here("R", "data_bundle.R"))
data_bundle_version <- 1

# Post-specific packages go here, and in R/packages.R
library(sf)        # spatial data held as a data frame with a geometry column
```

```{r}
#| label: load-data

# Small tidy files produced by R/02_clean_data.R live in data/
districts <- read_sf(here("posts", "welcome", "data", "districts.geojson"))

# How people live: the share of households that are a couple with children at
# home, the average number of people in a household, and the share of dwellings
# that are single-detached houses. 2021 census.
households <- read_csv(
  here("posts", "welcome", "data", "households.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Mother tongue and the language spoken at home, 2021 census.
language <- read_csv(
  here("posts", "welcome", "data", "language.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Where the people who live in each municipality go to work, 2021 census. Three
# rows per municipality, one per destination.
commuting <- read_csv(
  here("posts", "welcome", "data", "commuting.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Median household and median individual income from the 2021 census, which
# reports income earned in 2020, restated in 2026 dollars by 02_clean_data.R.
# Eight rows: the seven municipalities and the Region as a whole.
income <- read_csv(
  here("posts", "welcome", "data", "income.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
```

## First finding as a plain-language heading

<!-- One or two paragraphs, then one chart. -->

```{r}
#| label: districts
#| output: asis

# The seven municipal polygons, moved into EPSG:3161 - a projection made for
# Ontario, on which shapes this size keep their true proportions. The data is
# stored in plain latitude and longitude, which is convenient but draws a map
# slightly stretched, so the projection is chosen here rather than in the data.
districts_3161 <- st_transform(districts, 3161)

# Two labels need moving off the anchor stored in the data. It is the point
# furthest from any border, which is the roomiest spot but not always the one
# that looks centred once the words are drawn: Waterloo's sat half over its
# western border and Cambridge's ran past its eastern one. Metres east and
# north in EPSG:3161, arrived at by rendering the map and looking at it.
nudge <- tribble(
  ~district,    ~dx,    ~dy,
  "Waterloo",  1000,   1200,
  "Cambridge",   700, -2200
)

# Label positions. 02_clean_data.R worked out where each label should sit and
# stored it as a longitude and latitude; here that becomes a point, moves into
# the map's projection, and is turned back into plain x and y columns so the
# nudges above can simply be added to it.
#
# "Township" goes on a second line rather than after the name, so that even
# "North Dumfries Township" stays narrow enough to sit inside its own boundary.
labels <- districts |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("label_lon", "label_lat"), crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(3161) |>
  (\(points) bind_cols(
    st_drop_geometry(points),
    st_coordinates(points) |> as_tibble() |> set_names(c("x", "y"))
  ))() |>
  left_join(nudge, join_by(district)) |>
  mutate(
    # Every district that needs no nudge has no row in the table above
    x = x + replace_na(dx, 0),
    y = y + replace_na(dy, 0),
    label = if_else(
      district_type == "Township",
      paste0(district, "\nTownship"),
      district
    )
  )

p <- ggplot() +
  # Filled in the same two colours the bar chart uses, so a reader who has seen
  # one chart already knows which shapes are cities and which are townships.
  # The borders are white rather than a darker line: against filled shapes they
  # separate neighbours without drawing a second thing to look at, and around
  # the outside they disappear into the page, which leaves the Region as a
  # silhouette rather than a boxed-in diagram.
  geom_sf(
    data = districts_3161, aes(fill = district_type),
    colour = "white", linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = labels, aes(x = x, y = y, label = label),
    colour = "white", size = label_size, lineheight = 1.05, fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(City = dodgerblue, Township = habsred),
    guide = "none"   # the labels on the shapes say which is which
  ) +
  # datum = NA drops the graticule - the faint grid of latitude and longitude
  # lines coord_sf() draws by default - which this map has no use for.
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  labs(
    title = "The Region's three cities are almost entirely surrounded by the four townships",
    subtitle = "Waterloo Region, census subdivisions",
    caption = cwr_caption("Statistics Canada, 2021 census boundary files")
  ) +
  # theme_cwr() is built for charts with axes; a map wants none of them. Each
  # element is named individually because the theme sets them individually, and
  # a blanket axis.text would not override the more specific setting.
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
    axis.line.x = element_blank(), axis.line.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

cwr_figure(
  p, "fig-districts",
  alt = paste(
    "Outline map of Waterloo Region showing the borders of its seven municipalities,",
    "each labelled: the cities of Kitchener, Waterloo and Cambridge grouped together in",
    "the middle, ringed by Woolwich Township to the north, Wellesley Township to the",
    "north west, Wilmot Township to the south west and North Dumfries Township to the south."
  ),
  # The phone map is half as wide but its text is drawn at the same size, so the
  # three cities in the middle cannot hold their labels without a further
  # reduction; 0.60 is where they sit clear of each other and of the borders.
  height = 7.6, phone_height = 5.0, phone_text_scale = 0.60
)
```

## Second finding

```{r}
#| label: sizes
#| output: asis

# One row per municipality per measure. The three measures live in one column
# so that facet_wrap() can give each its own panel; pivot_longer() is what turns
# the three separate columns into that shape.
#
# The order is set once, on population, before the pivot - while there is still
# one row per municipality to sort. fct_reorder() sorts ascending and a
# horizontal bar chart draws the first level at the bottom, so the largest ends
# up on top. Because the order is baked into the factor, all three panels keep
# it, which is the point: the eye can travel across a row and stay on the same
# place.
# Roughly how many characters of label fit across one panel. Only used to work
# out which labels go inside their bars; see the comment where it is applied.
panel_chars <- 30

# The three measures: the column each comes from, the heading its panel carries,
# and how that heading should be said aloud. Keeping all three together means
# the alt text cannot drift from the panels, and lets the two differ where they
# should - a screen reader announces "km2" for km², so the spoken form spells
# the unit out.
measures <- tribble(
  ~column,             ~panel,                ~spoken,
  "population",        "Population",    "Population",
  "area_sq_km",        "Land area, km\u00b2",  "Land area in square kilometres",
  "density_per_sq_km", "People per km\u00b2",  "People per square kilometre"
)

panels <- districts |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(district = fct_reorder(district, population)) |>
  select(district, district_type, population, area_sq_km, density_per_sq_km) |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(population, area_sq_km, density_per_sq_km),
    names_to = "column", values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  left_join(measures, join_by(column)) |>
  mutate(
    # factor() fixes the panel order; left as characters the panels would come
    # out alphabetically
    measure = factor(panel, levels = measures$panel)
  ) |>
  # Each panel has its own scale, so "does this label fit inside its bar" has to
  # be asked panel by panel: a bar of 278 is nearly full width among areas and
  # invisible among populations.
  #
  # What decides it is the width of the text, not the size of the number. An
  # earlier version compared the bar against a fixed fraction of the longest bar
  # in its panel, which put "113" outside a bar with room for twice that, simply
  # because 113 is a small share of 327.
  #
  # So the label's width is estimated in the panel's own units. A panel is about
  # `panel_chars` characters wide at this font size - measured from a render
  # rather than derived, since it depends on the font and the panel's width -
  # and the longest bar covers all but the 20% expansion left for outside
  # labels. One character is therefore max(value) * 1.2 / panel_chars wide, and
  # a label needs its own length plus a space or so of padding to sit inside.
  group_by(measure) |>
  mutate(
    label = label_comma(accuracy = 1)(value),
    inside = value >= (nchar(label) + 1.5) * (max(value) * 1.2 / panel_chars)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

p <- ggplot(panels, aes(x = value, y = district, fill = district_type)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  # The baseline the bars grow from. theme_cwr()'s own x axis line is switched
  # off below, because with labels on the bars there is no axis to carry.
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label = label,
      # Inside the bar end, or just past it - hjust flips the text about its
      # anchor, and the anchor is the end of the bar either way
      hjust = if_else(inside, 1.15, -0.15),
      colour = if_else(inside, "white", "black")
    ),
    size = label_size * 0.8
  ) +
  # The colours above are literal colour names rather than groups to map, which
  # is what scale_colour_identity() means: use the value, do not look it up
  scale_colour_identity() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(City = dodgerblue, Township = habsred),
    guide = "none"   # the colours are explained by the bars themselves
  ) +
  # Room on the right for the labels that sit outside their bars
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.20))) +
  facet_wrap(vars(measure), nrow = 1, scales = "free_x") +
  # Stops a label that overhangs the panel edge from being cut off
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title = "The townships are very sparsely populated compared to the cities",
    subtitle = "Population density, 2025",
    caption = cwr_caption(
      c("Statistics Canada Table 17-10-0155-01",
        "the 2021 census boundary files"),
      credit = TRUE
    )
  ) +
  # Every bar carries its number, so the value axis and its gridlines are gone.
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    axis.line.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing.x = unit(1.4, "lines")
  )

# The figures in the alt text are built from the same rows the bars are drawn
# from, not typed out. Typed, they would be right today and quietly wrong the
# first time an estimate is revised - and wrong only for the readers who cannot
# see the chart to check it against.
alt_lines <- panels |>
  summarise(
    entries = paste(paste0(district, " ", label), collapse = ", "),
    .by = c(measure, spoken)
  ) |>
  mutate(line = paste0(spoken, ": ", entries)) |>
  pull(line)

cwr_figure(
  p, "fig-sizes",
  alt = paste0(
    "Three panels of horizontal bars, one row per municipality, ordered by ",
    "population, with the three cities in blue and the four townships in red. ",
    paste(alt_lines, collapse = ". "), "."
  ),
  height = 4.6, phone_height = 9.5,
  # Three panels side by side on a desktop will not fit across a phone, so the
  # phone version stacks them instead. Adding a facet replaces the one above.
  phone = list(facet_wrap(vars(measure), ncol = 1, scales = "free_x"))
)
```

```{r}
#| label: group-totals
#| include: false

# The chart these built is gone; the numbers are kept because the prose uses
# them - density_comp is the ratio quoted in the text. Everything here needs
# `measures` and `panel_chars`, which the chunk above defines.

# The same three measures as the chart above, with the seven municipalities
# collapsed into the two groups. `measures` and `panel_chars` are the ones
# defined in the chunk above, so the panel headings, their spoken forms and the
# label-fitting rule cannot drift between the two charts.
#
# Population and land area are sums. Density is not: averaging seven densities
# would give Wellesley the same weight as Kitchener and come out far too low.
# It has to be the group's people divided by the group's land, which is why it
# is worked out after the summarise() rather than carried through it.
group_totals <- districts |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  summarise(
    population = sum(population),
    area_sq_km = sum(area_sq_km),
    .by = district_type
  ) |>
  mutate(density_per_sq_km = population / area_sq_km)

group_panels <- group_totals |>
  # The bars are the plural of the type that colours them; fct_reorder() on
  # population puts the cities on top and holds that order across all three
  # panels, as in the chart above.
  mutate(
    group = fct_reorder(
      if_else(district_type == "City", "Cities", "Townships"),
      population
    )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(population, area_sq_km, density_per_sq_km),
    names_to = "column", values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  left_join(measures, join_by(column)) |>
  mutate(measure = factor(panel, levels = measures$panel)) |>
  # Same test as the chart above: whether the label's own width fits inside the
  # bar, asked panel by panel because each panel has its own scale.
  group_by(measure) |>
  mutate(
    label = label_comma(accuracy = 1)(value),
    inside = value >= (nchar(label) + 1.5) * (max(value) * 1.2 / panel_chars)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

density_comp <- group_panels |> 
  # Keep only the two density rows
  filter(column == "density_per_sq_km") |> 
  # Pick each value by its district_type and divide
  summarise(ratio = value[district_type == "City"] / value[district_type == "Township"]) |> 
  # Extract the single number so density_comp is a numeric value, not a tibble
  pull(ratio)
```

```{r}
#| label: households
#| output: asis

# Two measures, each with its own unit, so each panel gets its own scale and its
# own number format. The panel heading carries the unit wherever the label
# cannot: "3.4" says nothing on its own, "85%" says most of it.
# Roughly how many characters of label fit across one panel of a two-panel
# chart at this font size, the way `panel_chars` does for the three-panel one.
# Used by this chart and by the mother tongue chart below.
panel_chars_wide <- 45

household_measures <- tribble(
  ~column,                    ~panel,                                   ~accuracy, ~suffix,
  "average_household_size",   "Average people per household",            0.1,      "",
  "single_detached_percent",  "Single-detached houses, % of dwellings",  1,        "%"
)

household_panels <- households |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(average_household_size, single_detached_percent),
    names_to = "column", values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  left_join(household_measures, join_by(column)) |>
  mutate(
    measure = factor(panel, levels = household_measures$panel),
    label = label_number(accuracy = accuracy, suffix = suffix)(value)
  ) |>
  # Each panel is ordered by its own figures. ggplot2 has one discrete scale for
  # the whole chart, so a factor of place names can carry only one order; the way
  # round it is to make each bar's identity the place *and* its panel, sort that
  # combined key by value, and strip the panel off again in the scale below.
  # Drawn with a free y scale, each panel then shows only its own seven levels.
  mutate(row = fct_reorder(paste(district, measure, sep = "|"), value)) |>
  # Whether a label fits inside its bar, asked panel by panel because each panel
  # has its own scale. Same test as the population chart above, but a panel here
  # is wider - two panels to the page rather than three - so more characters fit
  # across it. Read off a render, as the other number was.
  mutate(
    inside = value >= (nchar(label) + 1.5) * (max(value) * 1.2 / panel_chars_wide),
    .by = measure
  )

p <- ggplot(household_panels, aes(x = value, y = row, fill = district_type)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  # The baseline the bars grow from; theme_cwr()'s own x axis line is switched
  # off below, because with labels on the bars there is no axis to carry.
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label = label,
      # Inside the bar end, or just past it - hjust flips the text about its
      # anchor, and the anchor is the end of the bar either way
      hjust = if_else(inside, 1.15, -0.15),
      colour = if_else(inside, "white", "black")
    ),
    size = label_size * 0.8
  ) +
  # The colours above are literal colour names rather than groups to map, which
  # is what scale_colour_identity() means: use the value, do not look it up
  scale_colour_identity() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(City = dodgerblue, Township = habsred),
    guide = "none"   # the same two colours as every other chart in the post
  ) +
  # Room on the right for any label that sits outside its bar
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.20))) +
  # Everything from the "|" on is the panel name carried by the sort key above,
  # and is not for reading.
  scale_y_discrete(labels = \(x) str_split_i(x, fixed("|"), 1)) +
  # Free on both axes: free on x because the two measures share no unit, free on
  # y because each panel holds its own order and so needs its own row labels.
  # label_wrap_gen() breaks a heading too wide for its panel onto a second line;
  # panel headings are drawn by the theme as plain text, so cwr_wrap() - which
  # emits <br> - would show its markup instead of acting on it.
  facet_wrap(vars(measure), nrow = 1, scales = "free",
             labeller = label_wrap_gen(22)) +
  # Stops a label that overhangs the panel edge from being cut off
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title = "Title: the finding, in one line",
    subtitle = "Subtitle: what is measured, for whom, and when<br>",
    caption = cwr_caption("Statistics Canada Table 98-10-0041-01", credit = TRUE)
  ) +
  # Every bar carries its number, so the value axis and its gridlines are gone.
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    axis.line.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing.x = unit(1.4, "lines")
  )

# Built from the plotted rows rather than typed, as above. Each line reads down
# its own panel, largest first, the way the bars are drawn.
alt_lines <- household_panels |>
  arrange(measure, desc(value)) |>
  summarise(
    entries = paste(paste0(district, " ", label), collapse = ", "),
    .by = measure
  ) |>
  mutate(line = paste0(measure, ": ", entries)) |>
  pull(line)

cwr_figure(
  p, "fig-households",
  alt = paste0(
    "Two panels of horizontal bars, one row per municipality, each panel ",
    "ordered by its own figures, with the three cities in blue and the four ",
    "townships in red. ",
    paste(alt_lines, collapse = ". "), "."
  ),
  height = 4.0, phone_height = 6.4,
  # Two panels side by side will not fit across a phone, so the phone version
  # stacks them. Adding a facet replaces the one above.
  phone = list(facet_wrap(vars(measure), ncol = 1, scales = "free",
                          labeller = label_wrap_gen(22)))
)
```

```{r}
#| label: income
#| output: asis

# The two measures: the column each comes from and the heading its panel
# carries. Kept in a table for the same reason as the chart above - the panel
# headings and the alt text are then built from one list and cannot drift
# apart. There is no separate spoken form here because both headings read
# aloud exactly as they are written.
income_measures <- tribble(
  ~column,                   ~panel,
  "household_income_2026",   "Household",
  "individual_income_2026",  "Individual"
)

income_panels <- income |>
  select(district, district_type, household_income_2026, individual_income_2026) |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(household_income_2026, individual_income_2026),
    names_to = "column", values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  left_join(income_measures, join_by(column)) |>
  mutate(
    measure = factor(panel, levels = income_measures$panel),
    # Each panel is ordered by its own figures rather than sharing one order,
    # so a place can sit seventh for household income and third for individual
    # income. That disagreement between the two panels is the point of putting
    # them side by side.
    #
    # ggplot2 has one discrete scale for the whole chart, so a factor of place
    # names can carry only one order. The way round it is to make each bar's
    # identity the place *and* its panel - "Kitchener|Median individual income"
    # - and sort that combined key by value. Drawn with a free y scale, each
    # panel shows only its own eight levels in its own order, and the scale
    # below strips the panel name off again before the label is drawn.
    # (tidytext::reorder_within() does exactly this. It is two lines here, so
    # the package is not worth adding.)
    #
    # fct_reorder() sorts ascending and a horizontal bar chart draws the first
    # level at the bottom, so the highest income ends up on top of its panel.
    row = fct_reorder(paste(district, measure, sep = "|"), value),
    # Rounded to the nearest hundred dollars. The census medians themselves are
    # rounded before publication, and multiplying by an index does not add
    # precision, so a figure to the dollar would be false exactness.
    label = label_currency(accuracy = 100, big.mark = ",")(value)
  )

p <- ggplot(income_panels, aes(x = value, y = row, fill = district_type)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  # The baseline the bars grow from; theme_cwr()'s own x axis line is switched
  # off below, because with labels on the bars there is no axis to carry.
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label = label,
      # Every label sits inside its bar end. The shortest bar here still holds
      # its label comfortably, so unlike the chart above there is no test for
      # which ones have to move outside.
      #
      # White on the blue and the red, black on the Region's silver: white on
      # that grey is a contrast ratio of about three to one, which is too
      # faint to read at this size.
      colour = if_else(district_type == "Region", "black", "white")
    ),
    hjust = 1.15,
    size = label_size * 0.8
  ) +
  # The colours above are literal colour names rather than groups to map, which
  # is what scale_colour_identity() means: use the value, do not look it up
  scale_colour_identity() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(City = dodgerblue, Township = habsred, Region = cowboysilver),
    guide = "none"   # the colours are explained by the bars themselves
  ) +
  # A little air at the bar ends so the longest bar does not touch the panel
  # edge. No room is needed on the right for outside labels, as there are none.
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))) +
  # Everything from the "|" on is the panel name carried by the sort key above,
  # and is not for reading.
  scale_y_discrete(labels = \(x) str_split_i(x, fixed("|"), 1)) +
  # Free on y, fixed on x. Free on y is what lets each panel hold its own
  # order, and it is why the second panel carries its own row labels: the rows
  # are no longer the same rows in the same places.
  #
  # x stays shared, which is the other point of the chart: a household is more
  # than one earner, and at one scale the individual bars come out visibly
  # shorter. Given its own scale - as the charts above do, where the measures
  # are people, square kilometres and a density - the second panel would look
  # like the first and that comparison would be lost.
  facet_wrap(vars(measure), nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Households and individuals in the townships outearn those in the cities",
    subtitle = "Median total income in 2020<sup>1</sup> of people living in private dwellings, 2026 dollars<sup>2</sup>",
    # One footnote, keyed to whatever in the title or subtitle needs it.
    caption = cwr_caption(
      c("Statistics Canada Tables 98-10-0057-01, 98-10-0070-01", "and 18-10-0004-01"),
      credit = TRUE,
      notes = c("latest year available, from 2021 census", "adjusted by the Ontario all-items CPI")
    )
  ) +
  # Every bar carries its number, so the value axis and its gridlines are gone.
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    axis.line.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing.x = unit(1.4, "lines")
  )

# Built from the plotted rows rather than typed, for the reason given above.
alt_lines <- income_panels |>
  # Each line reads down its own panel, highest first, as the bars are drawn
  arrange(measure, desc(value)) |>
  summarise(
    entries = paste(paste0(district, " ", label), collapse = ", "),
    .by = measure
  ) |>
  mutate(line = paste0(measure, ": ", entries)) |>
  pull(line)

cwr_figure(
  p, "fig-income",
  alt = paste0(
    "Two panels of horizontal bars, one row per municipality and one for ",
    "Waterloo Region as a whole, with the three cities in blue, the four ",
    "townships in red and the Region in grey. Each panel is ordered by its own ",
    "figures, highest at the top, and both are drawn to the same dollar scale. ",
    paste(alt_lines, collapse = ". "), "."
  ),
  height = 4.8, phone_height = 6.6,
  # Two panels side by side will not fit across a phone, so the phone version
  # stacks them. Adding a facet replaces the one above.
  phone = list(facet_wrap(vars(measure), ncol = 1, scales = "free_y"))
)
```


```{r}
#| label: language
#| output: asis

# The second measure is a share of a share - German or Pennsylvania German among
# those whose mother tongue is neither English nor French - which is why its
# heading starts "of those". Both are percentages, but of different denominators,
# so each panel keeps its own scale.
language_measures <- tribble(
  ~column,                           ~panel,
  "non_official_percent",            "Mother tongue not English or French, % of people",
  "german_percent_of_non_official",  "Of those, % with German or Pennsylvania German"
)

language_panels <- language |>
  # One order for both panels, set on the first. That is the whole point of this
  # chart: read across a row and the second panel disagrees with the first.
  mutate(district = fct_reorder(district, non_official_percent)) |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(non_official_percent, german_percent_of_non_official),
    names_to = "column", values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  left_join(language_measures, join_by(column)) |>
  mutate(
    measure = factor(panel, levels = language_measures$panel),
    label = label_number(accuracy = 1, suffix = "%")(value)
  ) |>
  # Same test as the household chart above, panel by panel.
  mutate(
    inside = value >= (nchar(label) + 1.5) * (max(value) * 1.2 / panel_chars_wide),
    .by = measure
  )

p <- ggplot(language_panels, aes(x = value, y = district, fill = district_type)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label = label,
      hjust = if_else(inside, 1.15, -0.15),
      colour = if_else(inside, "white", "black")
    ),
    size = label_size * 0.8
  ) +
  scale_colour_identity() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(City = dodgerblue, Township = habsred),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.20))) +
  # Free on x only: the two panels share one order, so they share one set of row
  # labels. Headings wrapped for the same reason as the chart above.
  facet_wrap(vars(measure), nrow = 1, scales = "free_x",
             labeller = label_wrap_gen(22)) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title = "Title: the finding, in one line",
    subtitle = "Subtitle: what is measured, for whom, and when<br>",
    caption = cwr_caption(
      "Statistics Canada Table 98-10-0180-01",
      credit = TRUE,
      notes = c(
        "Mother tongue is the language first learned at home in childhood and still understood",
        "German and Pennsylvania German counted together"
      )
    )
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    axis.line.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing.x = unit(1.4, "lines")
  )

alt_lines <- language_panels |>
  summarise(
    entries = paste(paste0(district, " ", label), collapse = ", "),
    .by = measure
  ) |>
  mutate(line = paste0(measure, ": ", entries)) |>
  pull(line)

cwr_figure(
  p, "fig-language",
  alt = paste0(
    "Two panels of horizontal bars, one row per municipality, both ordered by ",
    "the share whose mother tongue is neither English nor French, with the ",
    "three cities in blue and the four townships in red. ",
    paste(alt_lines, collapse = ". "), "."
  ),
  height = 4.0, phone_height = 6.4,
  phone = list(facet_wrap(vars(measure), ncol = 1, scales = "free_x",
                          labeller = label_wrap_gen(22)))
)
```

```{r}
#| label: commuting
#| output: asis

# A stacked bar rather than a lollipop, because these three numbers are parts of
# one whole - every worker who lives in the municipality is in exactly one of
# them - and a stack shows a share of the row at a glance where three separate
# dots would not.
commuting_bars <- commuting |>
  mutate(
    # Drawn in order of distance from home, nearest first, so every bar reads
    # left to right as "how far do people go".
    destination = factor(
      destination,
      levels = c("In their own municipality", "Elsewhere in the Region", "Outside the Region")
    ),
    # Ordered on the share who stay put. fct_reorder() sorts ascending and a
    # horizontal chart draws the first level at the bottom, so the municipality
    # whose workers are most self-contained ends up on top.
    district = fct_reorder(
      district,
      if_else(destination == "In their own municipality", percent, 0),
      .fun = max
    ),
    label = label_number(accuracy = 1, suffix = "%")(percent),
    # A segment narrower than about a tenth of the bar cannot hold a two-digit
    # percentage, so those go unlabelled rather than overhanging into their
    # neighbour. Read off a render; nothing here is that narrow yet, but the
    # numbers move when the census does.
    label = if_else(percent >= 10, label, "")
  )

p <- ggplot(commuting_bars, aes(x = percent, y = district, fill = destination)) +
  # reverse = TRUE stacks the first level at the left. Left to itself ggplot2
  # stacks factor levels from the right, which would put the longest journey
  # nearest the axis and read backwards.
  geom_col(width = 0.7, position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.5) +
  # position_stack() with vjust 0.5 puts each label in the middle of its own
  # segment rather than at the end of the bar.
  geom_text(
    aes(label = label), position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5, reverse = TRUE),
    colour = "white", size = label_size * 0.8
  ) +
  # Dark to light as the distance grows: the eye reads the ramp as distance
  # without being told. This is the one chart in the post where the colours mean
  # something other than city and township, which the legend has to carry.
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      `In their own municipality` = dodgerblue,
      `Elsewhere in the Region` = dodgerblue50,
      `Outside the Region` = cowboysilver
    )
  ) +
  # The bars fill the width by construction, so the axis says nothing the
  # segments do not.
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))) +
  labs(
    title = "Title: the finding, in one line",
    subtitle = "Subtitle: what is measured, for whom, and when<br>",
    fill = NULL,
    caption = cwr_caption(
      "Statistics Canada Table 98-10-0462-01",
      credit = TRUE,
      notes = "Workers with a usual place of work; people who work from home are counted in their own municipality"
    )
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    axis.line.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
  )

alt_lines <- commuting_bars |>
  mutate(entry = paste0(destination, " ", label_number(accuracy = 1)(percent), " per cent")) |>
  summarise(entries = paste(entry, collapse = ", "), .by = district) |>
  mutate(line = paste0(district, ": ", entries)) |>
  pull(line)

cwr_figure(
  p, "fig-commuting",
  alt = paste0(
    "One horizontal bar per municipality, each split into three parts: the ",
    "share of its workers who work in their own municipality, the share who ",
    "work elsewhere in Waterloo Region, and the share who work outside it. ",
    paste(alt_lines, collapse = ". "), "."
  ),
  height = 4.0, phone_height = 5.8,
  phone = list(
    # Three keys will not fit across a phone in one row, so they stack into a
    # column. That means moving the legend as well as turning it: theme_cwr()
    # floats it just above the panel, which reserves no height, so a column of
    # keys would be drawn straight over the first bars. "top" makes the plot
    # give it room instead.
    guides(fill = guide_legend(ncol = 1)),
    theme(
      legend.position = "top",
      legend.direction = "vertical",
      # legend.justification alone does nothing once the legend is in the top
      # strip; that strip has its own justification setting.
      legend.justification.top = "left"
    )
  )
)
```
